description.narrative: Sexual exploitation of children (SEC) is a grave violation of children’s rights and affects millions of children and youth annually, regardless of gender. No region, country or child is immune, though girls, boys and children with other gender identities face differing levels of risk to different manifestations of SEC depending on their intersectional vulnerability factors. It impacts heavily and long lastingly on their physical, emotional and mental well-being. It deprives children and youth of establishing healthy (sexual) relationships and from developing to the best of their potential. The SUFASEC programme is designed to combat SEC and will work in 12 countries in Latin America and South and South East Asia: Bangladesh, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Guatemala, India, Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, Philippines and Thailand.

The SUFASEC programme is designed to combat SEC by working towards the following long-term impact: “Children in all of their diversity are better protected from sexual exploitation.” This activity forms part of the SUFASEC programme. The long-term impact will be reached through three interlinking objectives that address different dimensions (social norms, assets/environments, and laws/policies/systems). 1. Children, youth and their communities successfully challenge social norms and harmful practices related to SEC 2. Children and youth have access to and are supported by strengthened assets and protective environments 3. Children and civil society meaningfully participate in holding duty bearers, including government and local authorities, accountable to their obligations towards improved (implementation of) laws, policies, and systems

The different stakeholder groups involved in the SUFASEC programme include: - Children and youth in all their diversity: A child-centred approach: children and youth are the most important stakeholders. When children/youth fall victim to SEC the physical and mental impact can be long lasting. The Alliance adheres to the UN definition of child (0-18 years) and youth (15-24 years)- Caregivers and Communities: Critical stakeholders in the community include parents, caregivers, community leaders, teachers, local Community Based Organisations (CBOs), social workers, and other community members involved in community based child protection mechanisms.- CSOs and CBOs: Local child protection organisations support and implement activities at community level, L&A towards national actors, and provide synergies of interventions.- Local and national governments: formulate, endorse and implement laws and public policies related to SEC- Private Sector: Travel and tourism orgs (e.g., large and small, hotels, transport), as well as ICT/ Digital Service Providers have interest to avoid SEC taking place within their value chain, and to avoid having their products and services used to facilitate SEC- International donors, Intergovernmental bodies, INGOs, Multilateral entities55: Targeted audiences and partners for evidence based regional and international lobbying- Dutch Stakeholders: NL Embassies in programme countries, MoFA, MoJ&S, to formalise the network for sustainable cooperation to end SEC and impunity of offenders. The Dutch Public- Media & Journalists: Investigative and reporting outlets in the Programme countries. Media and journalists in the Netherlands.

The focus of this indicator is the coordination with the Vice-Ministry of Tourism for the development of a national code of conduct for the private sector, linked to Travel and Tourism, in order to position the prevention of CSEC in Travel and Tourism, in articulation with the State.

Significant progress has been made in coordination with the Bolivian Police Gender Unit to reformulate its institutional gender policy, which will be in force between 2022 and 2026. As part of the process, awareness-raising strategies have been implemented in the country's main cities (La Paz, Cochabamba and Santa Cruz) and educational material has been developed with a preventive approach, including gender, ESNNA and digital violence. In addition, a digital platform with training resources for Gender Unit staff has been created. At the end of the period of validity, an evaluation of compliance with this policy is planned.

The Bolivian Vice-Ministry of Tourism convened the DTZ partner to address the issue of trafficking and smuggling in the tourist destination of Uyuni, especially due to cases linked to SEC in the surrounding municipalities. A work plan proposal emerged from this meeting, which is subject to evaluation and includes the socialisation of the model of safe destinations free of SEC - TT, with the objective of improving this tool and allowing the Vice-Ministry to replicate the model in other municipalities. During the meeting, the need to reformulate Law 292 was identified, which could involve the development of a code of ethics, the implementation of specific regulations or the creation of a resolution to address this demand. In this context, a work plan was presented that involves the development of technical roundtables to evaluate and build a code of ethics, taking as a reference ethical codes applied in other countries. In addition, progress has been made in the work and coordination with the Gender Unit of the Bolivian Police, with the proposal to reformulate the institutional gender policy.

The partner's lobbying capacities will be strengthened through articulation processes at regional level, through the development of research on the gaps in care for the Venezuelan migrant population, in coordination with Conexión and DCI-ECPAT. This research is essential for national and regional lobbying based on evidence. Advocacy processes will continue with the Vice-Ministry of Tourism and the Ministry of Justice, through the Plurinational Council on Trafficking in Persons.

In the area of political advocacy, prevention activities were carried out in coordination with the Plurinational Council against Trafficking and Smuggling of Persons. Through this effort, the shelter care model was shared with the Departmental Councils, also involving the community and children and adolescents in the activities included in the Annual Plan of this collegiate body. This work is closely coordinated with the Technical Secretariat, led by the Ministry of Justice, which has strengthened institutional relations and facilitated direct access to the competent authorities.

"The Bolivian partner, Fundación Munasim Kullakita, has 16 years of experience in the care, protection and prevention of CSEC. It has projects in various urban, rural and border municipalities in Bolivia. Due to their specialisation, they are part of the Plurinational Council against Human Trafficking in Bolivia, as technical assistants, a situation that allows them to coordinate with various Ministries (Justice, Government, Education, Tourism), Bolivian Police (Human Trafficking and Interpol Divisions), Governors' Offices and Municipalities on actions to benefit children and adolescents, and to advise these bodies on possible modifications or improvements to public policies related to CSEC. It is part of the commission for the modification of the law on human trafficking and related crimes, as well as in the modification of the Tourism Law for the adaptation of codes of conduct and to avoid SEC in travel and tourism.It works on the basis of a community-based ECO 2 approach that is implemented through the identification of opinion leaders and formal leaders, a process of training/education in leadership skills, decision-making, conflict resolution and others, the formation of local community protection committees and the recognition of these bodies by the authorities."

The work is focused on the LGTBIQ population, survivors of CSEC or at high risk, and the community approach with which the partner works will help to determine the real and concrete needs of this group. The challenge is to work with victims of CSEC from this population given the social taboos and the lack of experience and knowledge of protection services.

We did not achieve the target due to a change of focus towards the sexual diversity population (LGTBIQ) with whom we have reinforced training processes in business management and employability, adopting our community-based approach called ECO-2. This approach involves a bottom-up building process, based on the specific needs of the target population. The objective of the change was to contribute to the construction of the life plan of the target population.

We have established agreements with organizations such as Wiñay Wara (an independent, autonomous, self-managed, and feminist organization focused on youth), TST (Trans Sex Workers), and Otraf-Bolivia (an organization that defends the rights of trans women in the city of La Paz). The target population is mainly young people between the ages of 18 and 23, with a high school education, who identify as non-binary. Many of these people have been expelled from their families because of their gender identity, which has led them to form support networks within collectives and groups with whom they share identity and experiences.

This group is composed of SEC survivors and at high-risk, who will receive training as part of the comprehensive care (biological, psychological and legal) at the partner's shelter . The age range is from 14 to 21 years old, and they come from rural areas and other regions of the country. Many of them are victims of internal trafficking, and there is also a percentage of foreign adolescentes. This indicator will include training on SEC, Comprehensive Sexuality Education (CSE) and SRHR, reflecting a holistic approach. This will provide young women with a solid foundation to make informed decisions about their health and well-being.

We have given information on sexuality, HIV/AIDS, STIs, pregnancy and contraception to 60 girls between 14 and 21 years of age, who are SEC survivors and at high risk. The objective is to help them in the construction of their life project. In the SRHR approach we consider not only the biological aspects, but also the emotional-affective, social and cultural aspects of sexuality and reproduction, which are linked to SEC, as it is these aspects that are exploited by the aggressors or pimps. This holistic approach aims to empower these young women to make informed decisions about their sexual and reproductive health, and to build a safer and healthier future for themselves.

We work with girls and adolescents who are survivors and receive care at the shelter as part of the process of restoring their rights. They are girls between the ages of 13 and 18 from various rural and urban areas in different departments of Bolivia, as well as foreign adolescents. Most of them have a primary school education and belong to indigenous peasant communities. They also come from family backgrounds characterized by single-parent or dysfunctional structures. At the same time, this process has been extended to educational institutions located in peripheral areas of the regions where we work, with a school population aged between 12 and 18. This population has a high prevalence of internal migration from rural areas to urban centers and is characterized by single-parent families, most of whom work in the informal trade sector.

We provided information on SRHR, HIV/AIDS, STIs, pregnancy and contraception to 40 young men aged 16-22, who self-identify themselves as belonging to a high-risk population in terms of sexual and reproductive health. We also included information on types of violence against women. We have made substantial progress with them in recognising their SRHR, which can have a positive impact on their well-being and on preventing risks to their health and that of their partners.

We work mainly in educational units located in peripheral areas of the regions where we operate, reaching school-age adolescents between the ages of 12 and 18. This population is mostly characterized by being part of internal migration processes from rural areas to urban areas. They come from nuclear and single-parent families, generally linked to the informal sector of commerce or wage-earning jobs, such as transportation. We address issues such as sexuality, HIV/AIDS, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), pregnancy, and contraceptive methods. At the same time, we continue to actively involve the leaders of the Comprehensive Differentiated Care for Adolescents and Youth (AIDAJ), who are part of the Education Program of CIES, an organization specializing in the promotion of sexual and reproductive rights. These initiatives have been fundamental in eliminating cultural, social, and emotional barriers that have historically limited young men's access to sexual and reproductive health information.

These services will focus on addressing SRHR (Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights) issues in the context of diverse sexual and gender orientations, and it is hoped that these services will be accessed in the future with a foundation already in place for responsible and inclusive service delivery.

Currently, members of this association are part of the LGBT Collective of the Department of La Paz. These actions have made it possible to establish a link to responsibly address issues related to DSDR in the context of diverse sexual orientations, although they have not yet accessed services. Survivors who are in the process of family reintegration have been included. They have voluntarily chosen to access sexual and reproductive health services, thus guaranteeing the exercise of their rights in a safe and protected environment. Care is provided through a multidisciplinary approach that integrates medical, social, and psychological assistance, implemented in the Trampolín shelter, which allows for comprehensive intervention aimed at their recovery and empowerment. At the same time, the participation of girls and adolescents in vulnerable situations in socio-educational strategies, such as Espacio Abierto, has been promoted with the aim of strengthening their autonomy and preventing future scenarios of exploitation. Through specialized technical support, these adolescents have gained access to services at specialized institutions such as CIES and Marie Stopes.

We were able to reach 47 adolescent girls between the ages of 12 and 17 SEC survivors and at risk, who said they felt safe in the DSDR services they access. The specific care was in gynaecology where they also received Pap smears. This suggests that the services provided go beyond basic care and focus on specific aspects of reproductive health, such as early detection of cervical abnormalities. These services are part of strategic alliances with mainly private institutions specialising in DSDR. We are also coordinating with the few public agencies that provide this care.
